name: secure-logging
description: Log security events properly without leaking sensitive data like passwords, tokens, PII, or credit card numbers
author: community
content:
## Secure Logging

Logs are essential for security monitoring — but they're also a liability if they contain sensitive data (OWASP A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures).

### NEVER Log These
- Passwords or password hashes
- Session tokens, JWTs, API keys, or OAuth tokens
- Credit card numbers or CVVs
- Social Security Numbers or government IDs
- Full date of birth
- Encryption keys or secrets
- Request bodies containing file uploads
- Full database connection strings with credentials

### ALWAYS Log These (Security Events)
- Authentication successes and failures (with username, IP, timestamp)
- Authorization failures (who tried to access what)
- Input validation failures (potential attack probing)
- Application errors and exceptions (server-side only)
- Administrative actions (user creation, role changes, config changes)
- Data export or bulk access operations
- Rate limit violations
- Changes to security-sensitive settings

### Sanitization Rules
```python
# BAD — logs the full token
logger.info(f"User authenticated with token: {token}")

# GOOD — logs a safe prefix only
logger.info(f"User authenticated with token: {token[:8]}...")

# BAD — logs full request body which may contain passwords
logger.debug(f"Request body: {request.body}")

# GOOD — log specific safe fields
logger.debug(f"Login attempt for user: {request.body.get('email')}")
```

### PII Handling in Logs
- Hash or truncate PII before logging (email → `j***@example.com`)
- Use structured logging with explicit field selection — never dump entire objects
- Tag log fields containing PII so log aggregation tools can mask/filter them
- Set log retention policies aligned with data regulations (GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA)
- Encrypt log storage and transmission

### Log Format Best Practices
- Use structured logging (JSON) for machine-parseable output
- Include: timestamp, severity, service name, request ID, user ID (if available), event type
- Use UTC timestamps in ISO 8601 format
- Include correlation/request IDs for tracing across services

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-03-23T10:15:30.000Z",
  "level": "WARN",
  "service": "auth-service",
  "event": "login_failed",
  "request_id": "req_a1b2c3d4",
  "user_email_hash": "5e884898da28...",
  "ip": "192.168.1.1",
  "reason": "invalid_password",
  "attempt_count": 3
}
```

### Log Injection Prevention
- Sanitize user input before including in log entries
- Prevent newline injection (`\n`, `\r`) that could forge log entries
- Use parameterized logging, not string formatting

```python
# BAD — user can inject fake log entries
logger.info(f"User login: {username}")

# GOOD — structured logging prevents injection
logger.info("User login", extra={"username": username})
```

### Monitoring Alerts
Set up alerts for:
- Spike in authentication failures (brute force)
- Multiple authorization failures from same user/IP
- Unusual data export volumes
- New admin user creation
- Changes to security configuration
